extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for designing story structure and character (how they interrelate), building climaxes, and shaping a single controlling idea for film/teleplay/screenplay storytelling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain a single subject/passion
rubrics_metrics.description: Each tightly focuses his oeuvre on one idea, a single subject that ignites his passion, a subject he pursues with beautiful variation through a lifetime of work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask yourself what will keep your desire burning over many months. Great writers are not eclectic — pick a subject that sustains you. Examples: Hemingway's exploration of death; Dickens' recurring father-loss motif. Avoid writing to impress intellectual friends or critics; write in service of what you love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write in the genre you love
rubrics_metrics.description: So, in addition, ask: What's my favorite genre? Then write in the genre you love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Genre should be a constant source of reinspiration; every time you reread your script it should excite you. Do not write something because you think it will be socially important or win critical praise; be honest in genre choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish characterization from character
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterization is the sum of all observable qualities (age, IQ, dress, job, mannerisms). True Character is revealed in the choices a human being makes under pressure — the greater the pressure, the deeper the revelation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characterization = surface traits; Character = choices under pressure. Use behaviors and details to make the character credible, but understand that only pressured choice reveals core nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reveal true character through choices under pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: The only way to know the truth is to witness [a character] make choices under pressure to take one action or another in the pursuit of his desire.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pressure is essential — trivial choices reveal little. Use escalating dilemmas (examples: burning bus scene) to show who people really are. Show different possible outcomes (heroism, cowardice, unconscious prejudice) to give depth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character revelation: contrast/contraction with characterization
rubrics_metrics.description: The revelation of true character in contrast or contradiction to characterization is fundamental to all fine storytelling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If characterization and true character match with no contradiction, the role becomes predictable and boring. Use contrast (e.g., Bond's playboy façade vs. ruthlessness) to sustain audience interest over many stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principal characters require hidden dimensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The revelation of deep character in contrast or contradiction to characterization is fundamental in major characters. Minor roles may or may not need hidden dimensions, but principals must be written in depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design principal characters so their choices under pressure contradict or complicate their surface traits; secondary characters can be simpler if genre permits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character arc: inner change over the telling
rubrics_metrics.description: The finest writing not only reveals true character, but arcs or changes that inner nature, for better or worse, over the course of the telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show a progression from initial characterization through pressured choices to a transformed humanity by the climax (example: The Verdict's Frank Galvin). The arc must feel causally driven by events and choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of structure: build escalating pressures
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of STRUCTURE is to provide progressively building pressures that force characters into more and more difficult dilemmas where they must make more and more difficult risk-taking choices and actions, gradually revealing their true natures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design event structure as a series of escalating tests that force revealing choices; structure itself is the mechanism for revelation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of character: supply believable qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: The function of CHARACTER is to bring to the story the qualities of characterization necessary to convincingly act out choices. Put simply, a character must be credible: young enough or old enough, strong or weak, worldly or naive, educated or ignorant, generous or selfish, witty or dull, in the right proportions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters possess traits that make their actions believable in context. If traits contradict a planned climax, revise either characterization or plot for credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interdependence of character and structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Structure and character are interlocked. The event structure of a story is created out of the choices that characters make under pressure and the actions they choose to take, while characters are the creatures who are revealed and changed by how they choose to act under pressure. If you change one, you change the other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Altering an event can change a character (e.g., changing a pivotal honest-to-lying choice creates a wholly new character). Conversely, reinventing character requires redesigning the story so choices and events express the new nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Character-driven' is redundant — aim for appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: For this reason the phrase 'character-driven story' is redundant. All stories are 'character-driven.' Event design and character design mirror each other. The key is appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust complexity and depth of character to the genre and story needs rather than fetishizing 'character-driven' as a separate mode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adjust character complexity to genre
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative complexity of character must be adjusted to genre. Action/Adventure and Farce demand simplicity of character; stories of personal and inner conflict demand complexity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't overcomplicate characters in genres that rely on pace and plot; conversely, invest in deep character development for Redemption/Education/Inner-Conflict plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Climax/ending must be the most satisfying movement
rubrics_metrics.description: The final movement of a ballet, the coda of a symphony, the last act and its Story Climax — these culminating moments must be the most gratifying, meaningful experiences of all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Audiences judge films by their endings; if the final movement fails, the film will likely fail. Save the strongest emotion and meaning for the last act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus majority of story design on the climax
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the overwhelming effort that goes into designing story, 75 percent of that is focused on creating the climax of the last act. The story's ultimate event is the writer's ultimate task.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spend disproportionate time shaping the climax; if you haven't yet created a poetic, meaningful culminating climax, you don't yet have a story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure climax is credible to character (internal consistency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any aspect of characterization that undermines the credibility of [the climax] must be sacrificed. Plot is more important than characterization, but story structure and true character are one phenomenon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your climax demands physical or psychological capacities your protagonist lacks, either rework characterization (e.g., change age) or redesign the climax to preserve credibility (examples: Mojave chase must fit protagonist's abilities).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure as rhetoric — dramatize, don't explain
rubrics_metrics.description: Storytelling is the creative demonstration of truth. A story is the living proof of an idea... The means by which you bring the audience to your point of view resides in the very design you give your telling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove your idea through event structure and consequence rather than exposition. Let events dramatize ideas; avoid turning dialogue or narration into platforms for philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid explanatory dialogue and authorial explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Master storytellers never explain. Dialogue, the natural talk of characters pursuing desire, is not a platform for the filmmaker's philosophy. Explanations of authorial ideas, whether in dialogue or narration, seriously diminish a film's quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Express the story's meaning within the dynamics of events and choices; resist explicit thematizing or moralizing via speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for aesthetic emotion (union of idea and feeling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Story is the experience of aesthetic emotion — the simultaneous encounter of thought and feeling. When an idea wraps itself around an emotional charge, it becomes more powerful, more memorable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design moments where idea and emotion fuse (epiphanies) so the audience experiences meaning immediately. Different genres seek different intensities of aesthetic emotion (psycho-thriller strong; love story softer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise as generator of inspiration
rubrics_metrics.description: Premise, the idea that inspires the writer's desire to create a story, is often an open-ended question: 'What would happen if...?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Premises can come from anywhere (news, dream, craft problem). A premise need not remain sacred — if the evolving story diverges, follow the story. Writing is discovery; the premise awakens what waits within the writer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlling Idea defined and enforced
rubrics_metrics.description: A Controlling Idea is the story's ultimate meaning expressed through the action and aesthetic emotion of the last act's climax. It must be expressible in a single sentence and has two components: Value plus Cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the Controlling Idea (value + cause) to shape strategic, aesthetic choices — what to keep and what to cut. Mold the film around one clear idea; the clearer the organizing idea, the more meanings audiences will discover. Avoid packing too many ideas into one story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit the story to one clear idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The more beautifully you shape your work around one clear idea, the more meanings audiences will discover. Conversely, the more ideas you try to pack into a story, the more they implode upon themselves until the film collapses into rubble of tangential notions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore widely in drafts and discovery, but in revision shape the piece around a single Controlling Idea that can be stated as a sentence (Value + Cause). Use this as a pruning tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose honest, opinionated points of view
rubrics_metrics.description: If, to some people, a writer's final statement about life appears dogmatic and opinionated, so be it. Bland and pacifying writers are a bore. We want unfettered souls with the courage to take a point of view.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don't shy from asserting a strong Controlling Idea through the story's events; the aim is to create a living metaphor that convinces the audience through dramatized consequences.
